title: Trees as sampling models
dek: A phylogeny is a hypothesis about correlated genomes. The likelihood is a Markov process along branches, not a product over isolates.
story: Once isolates are related, the iid product ∏ f(yᵢ | θ) is the wrong joint. A tree T plus a substitution model Q defines a joint law on the alignment by running a Markov chain down branches and mixing at internal nodes. That joint is the phylogenetic likelihood L(T, Q, times | data).

Topology is a discrete parameter (or a posterior on trees). Branch lengths are usually in expected substitutions, not years, until a clock model maps them. Bootstrapping columns of the alignment is a common uncertainty ritual; it answers a different question than resampling independent outbreaks.

In TB, trees are used as pictures of lineage and as inputs to transmission inference. A pretty tree is not a likelihood. If the substitution model ignores recombination, long branches and mixed ancestry will still be drawn — confidently.
deepTitle: Pruning, and what the bootstrap is not
deep: Felsenstein pruning: the likelihood at a parent node is a sum over child states of emission × transition(Q, t). Complexity linear in sites × states × nodes, not exponential in isolates. That is why trees are computable and why misspecified Q still gives you a number.

Comparing two nested substitution models (HKY vs GTR extra parameters) can be an LRT if the trees and other bits are handled honestly — often they are not, because T is itself estimated. AIC on a fixed tree is a partial comparison. Posterior model probabilities need priors on trees, which are a research field, not a checkbox.

Recombination: a single tree is the wrong geometry when different genomic windows have different ancestries. Networks, ancestral recombination graphs, or “don’t pretend this is a tree” are the adult moves in a recombining region.
Independence of sites is another product you may not have (RNA structure, mutational hotspots). Composite likelihoods still produce peaks; SEs need sandwich or block bootstrap.

formulas.label: Tree likelihood (sketch)
formulas.expression: L(T, Q | alignment) = P(alignment | T, Q)
formulas.note: A joint over correlated tips, computed by pruning, not by iid isolates.

formulas.label: Branch transition
formulas.note: t in expected substitutions. A clock will later map t to years.

visual.caption: A tree as nested correlation: a root process splits, each branch runs a substitution Markov chain, tips are the observed genomes. Isolates in a clade are dependent because they share the path to the clade ancestor — the opposite of an iid product.

example.title: Two outbreak genomes, one likelihood
example.setup: Two isolates differ by 3 SNPs. An iid Bernoulli-per-site model treats 3/genome-length as if n = sites. A tree model treats them as a short shared branch plus two tiny terminal branches.

steps.title: Wrong product
steps.body: ∏_sites f(y_site | π) with independent isolates double-counts the shared history. SEs on π collapse.

steps.title: Tree joint
steps.body: One short internal branch explains most of the similarity. The data for a substitution rate are closer to “one outbreak” than to “two independent patients × 4 Mb.”

steps.title: Still a model
steps.body: If the three SNPs are in a recombined patch, even the tree joint is wrong. Look at the window, do not only look at the cartoon.

example.takeaway: The phylogenetic likelihood is a joint. Using it as a picture without writing P(data | T, Q) is decoration.

check.prompt: A phylogenetic likelihood differs from an iid-isolate product because:
choices: Tips share ancestral paths, so the joint does not factor over isolates
check.answer: Tips share ancestral paths, so the joint does not factor over isolates
check.why: That is the whole point of writing P(alignment | T, Q).

check.prompt: Two-state Jukes–Cant-style sketch: P(same state | t) = 0.5 + 0.5 e^{−2t}. At t=0 this equals:
check.why: e^0=1, so 0.5+0.5=1. Zero branch length means no change. As t→∞ it goes to 0.5.

whyWrong.0: That would be a forced change.

check.prompt: On the tree hierarchy, why do clade nodes sit above tips?
choices: Because clades are observed like fasta files
Because shared internal branches are the dependence the iid product forgot
Because Q lives only at the tips
check.answer: Because shared internal branches are the dependence the iid product forgot
check.why: The plate is nested correlation, the hierarchical-model cousin with a tree index.
